title: From Google to ChatGPT: How Patients Are Choosing Their Aesthetic Experts Now
excerpt: The way patients find an aesthetic doctor or clinic is changing.

children.text: The way patients find an aesthetic doctor or clinic is changing.

For years, the digital patient journey was relatively predictable. Someone heard about a treatment, searched Google, looked at a few clinic websites, read reviews and perhaps checked Instagram before booking.
That journey is now far more fragmented.

A patient might discover a doctor through TikTok, see them quoted in an online article, look at their Instagram, ask ChatGPT about the treatment they're considering and then Google the doctor's name before making contact.
For aesthetic businesses, that changes what it means to have a strong online presence.
Your website is no longer the whole story
Your website still matters enormously.
But it is only one part of what a prospective patient sees when researching you.
Search your own name and look at the wider picture.
What appears?
Media coverage, interviews, social profiles, reviews, videos, podcasts, industry awards and third-party mentions can all contribute to the impression someone forms before they ever visit your clinic.
In many cases, what other people say about you can be just as influential as what you say about yourself.
That makes your wider digital footprint increasingly important.
Patients are researching, not simply searching
Consumers have become much more sophisticated in the way they research aesthetic treatments.
They aren't necessarily typing "best aesthetic clinic near me" and booking the first result.

They may want to know which treatment is best for a particular concern, whether a trend they've seen on TikTok is safe, what questions they should ask a practitioner or which type of specialist they should see.
AI is adding another layer to this behaviour.
Instead of entering a few keywords into a search engine, people can now ask detailed questions and receive conversational answers that help them understand a subject before deciding what to do next.
That means businesses need to think beyond simply ranking for a handful of keywords.
Reputation exists across the internet
This is why authority is becoming so important.
If your expertise is consistently represented across credible sources, it creates a much stronger online picture than your own website could create alone.
Press coverage matters here.
So do podcasts, expert articles, interviews, professional profiles, awards, educational content and other credible references to your work.
None should be viewed in isolation.
Together, they help establish who you are, what you specialise in and why somebody should trust you.
Social media still plays an important role
The rise of AI doesn't mean Instagram, TikTok or other social platforms suddenly become irrelevant.
Quite the opposite.
Social media allows a prospective patient to see how you communicate, understand your approach and get a sense of the person behind the professional profile.
A patient may discover you somewhere else entirely and use Instagram as part of their final research.
This is why consistency matters across every platform.
Your website might say you're a leading expert in natural-looking aesthetics, but does the rest of your online presence support that positioning?
Think about your digital reputation, not individual platforms
The biggest shift is that businesses can no longer think about Google, PR, social media, AI and their website as completely separate things.
Patients don't.
They move between them.
The strongest aesthetic brands will therefore build an online reputation that makes sense wherever someone encounters them.
Because whether a patient first finds you through Google, Instagram, Vogue, a podcast or ChatGPT, the ultimate question they're trying to answer is exactly the same:
Can I trust this person?

title: How AI decides who to trust
excerpt: AI-powered search works differently from traditional search engines.

children.text: AI-powered search works differently from traditional search engines.
Rather than simply matching keywords, AI systems analyse information from across the web to understand who appears to be a credible source on a particular topic.
They look for consistent signals that demonstrate expertise, authority and trust.
These signals can include:
Mentions in trusted media publications.
Educational content published on your website.
Reviews and testimonials.
Professional profiles and credentials.
Speaking engagements and conference appearances.
Podcast interviews.
Industry awards and recognition.
Consistent information across multiple platforms.
The stronger and more consistent these signals are, the easier it is for AI systems to understand who you are, what you specialise in and why your business is a credible source of information.
Why third-party credibility matters
One of the reasons PR has become even more valuable is because it creates independent, third-party validation.
Anyone can say they're the best at what they do on their own website.
Patients expect that.
Search engines and AI systems understand that your website is where you tell your own story.
However, when respected publications, journalists and industry platforms feature you as an expert, that's an independent signal that others recognise your knowledge and expertise.

A feature in titles such as Vogue, Tatler or the Daily Mail isn't just valuable because thousands of people may read it. These publications have built significant authority over many years, and being quoted within trusted editorial content strengthens your overall digital footprint.
Of course, PR is only one piece of the puzzle. Reviews, educational content, professional profiles and other trusted mentions all contribute to your online authority.

But PR has a unique advantage because it combines two powerful benefits. It increases your visibility with potential patients today while also creating credible, third-party mentions that continue strengthening your online authority over time.
Your website is still your foundation
Your website remains one of the most important assets your clinic owns.
It's where patients learn about your treatments, your experience and your approach.
But your website is only one part of your digital reputation.
Think of it this way.
Your website tells people who you are.
Third-party sources help reinforce why they should believe it.
The clinics that build the strongest online authority are those that combine excellent website content with independent credibility across the wider internet.

That's why the most successful businesses don't rely on one marketing channel alone. They invest in content, SEO, PR, reviews and brand building together, creating a reputation that's visible wherever potential patients, and increasingly AI-powered search tools, are looking.

title: How to Build Authority in Aesthetics
excerpt: Being exceptional at what you do isn't always enough.

children.text: Being exceptional at what you do isn't always enough.

In today's aesthetics industry, patients have more choice than ever before. They aren't just choosing practitioners based on qualifications or price. They're looking for people they trust, people they recognise, and people who consistently demonstrate expertise.

That doesn't mean simply being the loudest voice online. Visibility without credibility doesn't build authority. The practitioners who stand out are those who combine genuine skill with a strong reputation, consistently sharing valuable knowledge and positioning themselves as trusted experts in their field.

After more than 20 years working in public relations, and over a decade specialising in aesthetics, I've seen first-hand that the businesses which grow the fastest aren't always those with the biggest marketing budgets. They're the ones that invest in building trust and authority over time.
What does authority actually mean?
Authority isn't about becoming famous, or having the biggest following.
It's about positioning yourself as a trusted expert in your field.

When potential patients discover you online, they immediately feel reassured by what they see. They find educational content, credible media coverage, industry recognition and consistent messaging that reinforces your expertise.
That visibility creates trust.

Trust is one of the most valuable assets you can have in aesthetics because patients are making decisions about their appearance, their confidence and, ultimately, their health. They want to know they're in safe, experienced hands.

Building authority doesn't just improve your reputation. It strengthens your online presence, supports your SEO, increases your visibility in AI-powered search results, and gives prospective patients more confidence to book with you.
The biggest misconception about PR
One of the biggest misconceptions I hear is that PR is going to transform a business overnight.
It won't.
PR isn't a quick fix and it isn't about one magazine feature suddenly filling your diary with patients.

The real value of PR is that it helps build your brand over time. Every piece of media coverage, every expert comment, every podcast interview, every speaking opportunity and every educational article becomes another signal of credibility.
Over time, those signals compound.

Your online presence becomes stronger, your reputation grows, patients begin to recognise your name, and journalists, conference organisers and industry peers become more familiar with your expertise.
Like any successful brand, authority is built through consistency, not one-off moments.

title: The Aesthetics Industry Has a Trust Problem
excerpt: Aesthetics has never been more visible. Treatments that were once discussed mainly in clinics are now all over TikTok, Instagram and the wider media.

children.text: Aesthetics has never been more visible.
Treatments that were once discussed mainly in clinics are now all over TikTok, Instagram and the wider media.
In many ways, that's a good thing. Patients are more informed, more curious and much more likely to do their research before deciding on a treatment.
But there's another side to it.
There is now so much information out there that it can be incredibly difficult for patients to know who to trust.

A qualified doctor can be explaining the science behind a treatment in one video, while the next person on someone's feed might be confidently giving completely inaccurate advice. To the average person watching, both can look convincing.
For credible doctors, clinics and brands, simply telling people you're an expert isn't enough anymore. You need to give them reasons to believe it.
Anyone can look like an expert online
Social media has made it possible for anyone to have a voice, which has brought plenty of positives. But it has also made the line between expertise and influence much less clear.
A large following can make someone appear authoritative. A beautifully produced video can look credible. And a strong opinion can spread incredibly quickly, whether it's accurate or not.
We see this constantly in aesthetics.

Treatments become trends almost overnight. Before-and-after pictures are shared without much context. Complicated medical subjects are reduced to 30-second videos. Treatments can be made to look like they're suitable for everyone when, of course, they're not.
For genuine experts, this creates a completely different challenge.
You're no longer just competing for attention with other doctors or clinics. You're competing with everything a patient is seeing online.
Patients are asking more questions
The positive side is that patients are becoming much more aware of this.

Many aren't simply seeing a treatment on TikTok and immediately booking it. They're researching the doctor. They're reading reviews. They're looking at qualifications. They're searching Google, reading articles and comparing what different experts are saying.
Increasingly, they want to know not just what you offer, but why they should trust you.
And that's why credibility has to exist beyond your own website and social media.
Anyone can call themselves a "leading expert" in an Instagram bio.
It's much harder to build a reputation that is backed up by respected media, professional recognition, industry events, podcasts, awards and other independent sources.
What other people say about you matters
This is one of the reasons I believe PR has become even more valuable within aesthetics.
There is a big difference between telling people you're an expert and having other credible people and platforms recognise you as one.

Being asked for your opinion by a respected journalist, invited to speak at an industry event or interviewed about your specialist subject gives you a level of independent credibility that your own marketing can't create in quite the same way.
Of course, being featured in the press doesn't automatically make somebody a great doctor. And a big media profile will never replace qualifications, experience or good patient care.
But when genuine expertise is consistently backed up by credible third parties, it gives patients another reason to trust what they're seeing.
Education is becoming part of your reputation
The strongest experts aren't only talking about the treatments they offer.
They're educating people.

They explain when a treatment might be right and when it might not be. They talk about limitations as well as benefits. They challenge misinformation. They're prepared to say that the treatment everyone is suddenly talking about isn't necessarily right for everyone.
And I think patients really notice that.
There is something incredibly reassuring about an expert who isn't trying to sell you everything.
In aesthetics, where someone is making decisions about their face, body and health, that trust matters enormously.
Trust has to be earned
The aesthetics industry certainly doesn't have a visibility problem.
There are more treatments, more content, more opinions and more people competing for attention than ever before.
The challenge for patients is working out who is genuinely credible.
For doctors, clinics and brands, the answer isn't to shout louder or post more for the sake of it.

It's to build a reputation that holds up when someone starts doing their research. Through the information you share, the way you communicate, your experience, your results and the credible third parties willing to recognise your expertise.
Because in an industry where almost anyone can look like an expert online, being someone people genuinely trust is becoming more valuable than ever.

title: The Rise of the Doctor as a Personal Brand
excerpt: There was a time when the clinic was the brand.

children.text: There was a time when the clinic was the brand.
Patients remembered the clinic name, the location and perhaps the treatment they had received. The individual doctor or practitioner often sat behind that identity.
That is changing.
Today, some of the strongest brands in aesthetics aren't clinics at all. They're people.
Patients follow doctors on Instagram, watch their videos, listen to their opinions, read their interviews and become familiar with their approach long before they ever walk through the clinic door.
And in an industry where trust is so important, knowing and understanding the person behind the brand matters.
For doctors and practitioners, personal branding is no longer simply about becoming more visible online. Done properly, it can become one of the most valuable assets in their career.
Patients want to know who is treating them
Aesthetics is an unusually personal industry.
Patients aren't simply buying a product. They're trusting another person with their face, body or skin.
Qualifications and experience are incredibly important, but patients increasingly want to know more than what appears on a doctor's CV.

They want to understand how that person thinks. What do they believe makes a good result? Which trends do they disagree with? What would they never recommend? How do they approach ageing, injectables or skin health?
This is where personal branding can be incredibly powerful.
By regularly sharing your expertise, opinions and approach, you're allowing potential patients to get to know you before they've even met you.
That familiarity builds trust. And when somebody is deciding who they are going to trust with their appearance, it can make a significant difference.
Personal branding isn't about becoming an influencer
This is where personal branding is often misunderstood.
It doesn't mean posting constantly, sharing every part of your life or trying to build millions of followers.
But there's also no getting away from the fact that social media is a huge part of how people discover and connect with experts today.

Some of the most recognised aesthetic doctors have built audiences that extend far beyond their clinics. In some cases, they have become well-known public figures in their own right, appearing regularly in the media, on television, at events and across social platforms.
That doesn't make them any less of a doctor. Their medical expertise remains at the heart of their reputation. What they've done is build a recognisable name around that expertise.
And you don't need hundreds of thousands of followers to do the same.
A strong personal brand is about clarity and consistency. People should understand your expertise, your philosophy, your opinions and what you stand for.
Social media is an important part of that, but so are press coverage, speaking engagements, podcasts, educational content, television appearances and industry events.
The aim isn't necessarily fame. It's becoming recognised by the people who matter to your career and your business.
Your opinion is part of your expertise
Qualifications establish that you're capable of doing the job.
They don't necessarily tell people how you think.

The doctors who become recognised voices within their field are often those willing to contribute an opinion. They can explain why they disagree with a trend, what they're seeing among patients or how they believe their speciality is changing.
That doesn't mean being controversial for attention. It means contributing something useful to the conversation.

After years of working with medical experts in PR, I've seen how powerful this can be. Journalists remember the people who give them an interesting perspective, not simply the people with the longest list of qualifications.
Over time, those opinions become part of what you're known for.
You are investing in something you own
There is another reason I think doctors should take personal branding seriously.
You're investing in yourself.
Clinics can change. Careers evolve. You may move country, launch another business or decide that you want to do something completely different alongside clinical practice.
Your personal brand travels with you.

Perhaps one day you want to launch your own skincare line. You might be approached for a brand partnership, television opportunity, book, podcast, speaking engagement or ambassador role. You might decide to open another clinic or build an entirely new business.
A strong personal brand can open doors that may not even exist for you yet.
Your reputation can travel further than your clinic
None of this means the clinic brand becomes unimportant.
A strong clinic brand and a strong personal brand can make each other more valuable.
But increasingly, patients connect with people before they connect with businesses.

The doctors who understand this aren't trying to become influencers. They're building recognition around their expertise, investing in their reputation and creating opportunities that extend beyond the treatment room.
The future of aesthetics will still be built on expertise.
But the experts who become most recognised will increasingly be those willing to step out from behind the clinic name and let people understand who they are, what they know and what they stand for.

title: Why One Vogue Feature Won’t Transform Your Business, And What Will
excerpt: Getting featured in Vogue is exciting. It’s a publication almost every beauty, aesthetics and wellness brand would love to appear in, and securing that level of coverage is absolutely something worth

children.text: Getting featured in Vogue is exciting. It’s a publication almost every beauty, aesthetics and wellness brand would love to appear in, and securing that level of coverage is absolutely something worth celebrating.
But will one Vogue feature transform your business overnight? Very unlikely.
That doesn’t mean PR has become less valuable. In many ways, I believe it has become more valuable. What has changed is how that value shows up.
Years ago, a top-tier magazine feature could create an immediate spike in enquiries. Today, the impact is often much bigger than the bookings that arrive in the days after an article is published.

When your name, clinic or brand is consistently featured across credible third-party websites, you are building a digital footprint that extends far beyond your own social media channels. Those independent mentions can strengthen your search presence, create valuable backlinks and give both potential patients and online platforms more evidence of who you are and what you are known for.

This becomes particularly important as people increasingly use AI platforms such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini to research businesses, treatments and experts. These systems can draw on information published across the wider web, which makes credible third-party coverage an increasingly important part of your online authority.

So while someone might first discover you on Instagram, hear you on a podcast and later Google your name, PR plays a different role. It gives you something your own marketing cannot create in quite the same way: independent credibility.
PR is no longer just about who reads the article
Traditionally, the value of a piece of press coverage was largely measured by the audience of the publication.
That audience still matters, but it is no longer the whole story.

A piece of coverage can live online for years. It can appear when somebody searches your name, provide a backlink to your website, be shared across your own channels and contribute to the wider body of information about you or your business online.
This means the value of an article can continue long after the issue has disappeared from the newsstand.
It’s also why consistency matters.

One Vogue feature is impressive. But if a search for your name reveals credible coverage across Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, Forbes, national newspapers and respected industry titles, the picture becomes much more powerful.
You are no longer simply telling people that you are an expert. There is independent evidence supporting it.
Social media and PR do very different jobs
This is where I think businesses sometimes get confused.
If patients are spending so much time on Instagram and TikTok, why not simply focus all your attention there?
Because social media is largely what you say about yourself.
PR is what credible third parties are saying about you.

You can create brilliant content, build a large following and explain your expertise every day on Instagram. All of that is valuable. But an independent journalist choosing to include your opinion in an article provides a different type of credibility.
The strongest brands don't choose between PR and social media. They use them together.
A Vogue feature becomes an Instagram post. An expert quote becomes a video discussion. A journalist request becomes an opportunity to demonstrate your knowledge to a completely new audience.
Each channel strengthens the others.
The real value is in consistency
The biggest mistake is expecting one piece of coverage to do all the work.
PR builds momentum.

The more consistently your name appears alongside your area of expertise, the stronger the association becomes. Patients begin to recognise you. Journalists become familiar with you. Search results become stronger. Your online reputation grows.
And increasingly, that digital reputation matters to the platforms people are using to discover and research experts.
This is why I would rather see a client consistently featured in credible media throughout the year than secure one enormous feature and then disappear for six months.
So, does the Vogue feature still matter?
Absolutely.
But don't judge its success purely by how many people call your clinic the following morning.
Its real value is much bigger than that.
Press coverage builds third-party credibility, strengthens your digital presence and creates independent signals of expertise that your own marketing simply cannot replicate.
One Vogue feature is fantastic.
A consistent body of credible media coverage is what builds authority.
